The 1860 census of George Ackerman's household has been fully linked and built into the tree. Each link is rated "probably" rather than "certainly" because the 1860 census is the only research record so far attached to any of these people, with no independent second source yet to corroborate the identities. One important gap to flag: Catherine Ackerman, George's wife, does not appear in the extracted census assertions at all — no wife or mother role was recorded. This could mean she had died before 1860, was living elsewhere and enumerated separately, or possibly that the household belongs to a different George Ackerman. No parent-child edge was written from Catherine to the children because this record gives no basis for it. The two advisory warnings about unstandardised birthplaces on George and Catherine were there before this work and do not affect the conclusions.

The next step is to search for additional records — a marriage record for George and Catherine, an earlier census, or vital records for the children — to corroborate these identities and, if Catherine is confirmed as the children's mother, to add her as parent in the tree.

Here is what the person-evidence subagent did and found:

**Household linked and tree built out from the 1860 census (assertions a_001–a_007):**

- **Margaret Ackerman** — new person added to the tree; born about 1854 in Pennsylvania (aged 6 in 1860); parent-child edge created from George to Margaret.

Because the 1860 census does not record family relationships explicitly, both parent-child links are rated **"probably"** rather than "certainly" — they rest on household position and shared surname.

**Confidence caveat:** All eight new identity links were written, but the two children's status is "probable" pending corroboration.

---

**Open matter to investigate:**
Catherine Ackerman (George's wife, died 1884) does **not appear** in the extracted census record. She could have been enumerated separately, been temporarily absent, or this could belong to a different George Ackerman household. This should be resolved before treating the census as fully establishing the household.

**Recommended next step:** Search a later census, a death certificate, or a baptism register that places Henry and Margaret under both George *and* Catherine — this would raise the parent-child conclusions from "probably" to "certainly" and account for Catherine's absence.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

Question: q_001 (when and from where in Germany did Hermann Gaetjen immigrate; tree I1 Hermann, husband of I4 Amelia Nichols, father of I2 Henry Joseph b. 5 May 1878 San Francisco and I3 Amelia Otillie b. 23 Aug 1883 California).
Link these to the right person in the tree:
- src_001, assertions a_001 to a_009: 1875 San Francisco Great Register, Hermann Gatjen, 21, b. Germany, fireman, 5 Cook Street, naturalized 13 Aug 1875, California 4th District Court.
- src_002, assertions a_010 to a_014: Germans to America Index, Herm Gaetjen, b. 1854 Prussia, arrived New York 2 Jun 1871.
Decide identity yourself with same_person scoring. Context: other Hermann Gaetjens lived in California (one b. 1873, naturalized San Francisco 1900, d. 1957; one b. 1827, d. 1899 Butte County). I1's only birth fact (about 1859) is unsourced. If the evidence does not support linking either persona to I1, put it on a separate stub and say so.

agent_returns.text:
No warnings on I1. No facts were copied from either record (namesake cap prohibits it at `speculative`), so the tree person is unchanged and clean.

---

Both records were linked — only tentatively — to Hermann Gaetjen, your tree subject. The 1875 San Francisco Great Register and the Germans to America passenger index both describe a man named Hermann Gaetjen (or the variant spelling Gatjen) born in Germany around 1854 who was living in San Francisco in 1875, three years before his son Henry Joseph was born there. The two records fit each other perfectly — someone arriving in New York from Germany in 1871 and reaching San Francisco by 1875 is a completely natural path for the period — and neither of the two other California Hermann Gaetjens on file could be this man (one was barely a toddler in 1875, the other was nearly fifty and died in a different county). That said, both records carry a birth year of about 1854, while the family tree currently shows Hermann born about 1859; that five-year gap matters, though the 1859 date turns out to be just a rough modern estimate with no document behind it, so the records are more likely correcting a guess than describing a different person. Despite all of that, the links had to be recorded as only possible rather than probable, because the research database knows two other men named Hermann Gaetjen lived in California and cannot automatically rule them out from these single-person records alone — there is no co-listed family member or shared address to lock the connection to your Hermann. The links are saved and the evidence is fully recorded; nothing was written onto Hermann's tree profile yet. To lift these from "possible" to "probable," the next step is finding a document that connects this 1875 registrant to Amelia Nichols or to one of the children — a marriage record, a city directory entry, or a birth registration for Henry Joseph — which would tie the Great Register persona unmistakably to your family.

| pe_010 | a_027 → father side | I1 | 0.97 | Father as spouse of Amelia Nichols |
| pe_011 | a_027 → mother side | I4 | 0.96 | Amelia Nichols as spouse of Hermann Gaetjen |

**Why all `probable` and not `confident`:** The formal person_evidence section had zero entries before this run. No other record is yet formally linked to I1, I3, or I4 through the pe_ system, so the independent-corroboration requirement for `confident` cannot be met. All three matches are qualitatively strong (scores 0.95–0.97, name and relationship fit exact), but identity certainty remains `probable` until a second independently-sourced record is linked to each person.

**Namesake exclusion (I1):** ns_002 (born 1827, died 1899) cannot appear in a 1913 record. ns_001 (born 1873, San Francisco) is excluded because the record's father is married to Amelia Nichols and is the father of Amelie Ottilie — a family structure that belongs to I1 and no other recorded Hermann Gaetjen.

**Materialization:** I3 gained an alternative name spelling ("Amelie Ottilie Gaetjen") and a source reference on her birth fact from this marriage record. I1 and I4 each gained a source reference. No new conflicts were surfaced.

**Person warnings:** I1 and I4 are clean. I3 has a pre-existing advisory warning: a 1935 Residence fact carries a non-standard place value. This predates this run and is unrelated to the links just created.

The 1913 San Francisco marriage certificate for Amelia Gaetjen and William Fralich has been matched to its three family members: the bride herself, her father Hermann Gaetjen, and her mother Amelia Nichols. Each match is rated "probably" correct — the names, locations, and family relationships all fit cleanly, the two other men named Hermann Gaetjen in the files are ruled out (one died in 1899 and one was a different family entirely), but no second independent document has yet been formally connected to any of these three people, so the matches cannot yet be called definite. quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The person-evidence agent has completed a full audit of this link. Here is what it found:

### The Verdict: Tier Is Defensible, But the Rationale Is Too Thin

The `confident` rating is **substantively justified** — the corroborating evidence is there — but the rationale as currently written does not prove it. A reviewer reading pe_005 in isolation cannot audit whether the tier was earned.

---

### What Supports `confident`

- **Name match:** "Patrick Flynn" on the death certificate matches I1 exactly
- **Death date and county:** 12 March 1908, Schuylkill County, PA — aligns with the tree's own death fact for I1
- **Birth year:** ~1845 (from age-at-death) matches the census-derived birth year — gap = 0 years
- **Independent corroboration from two different sources:**
  - pe_001 (1850 U.S. Census) — Patrick Flynn, Schuylkill County, PA → I1
  - pe_004 (1860 U.S. Census) — Patrick Flynn, Schuylkill County, PA → I1
- **No competing candidate** named Patrick Flynn born ~1845 in Schuylkill County appears in the evidence base

---

### Four Gaps in pe_005's Rationale

| Gap | Impact |
|-----|--------|
| **match_score is null** — `same_person` was never called | Audit trail is incomplete; score should be obtained |
| **Mandatory check lines absent** — no date check or residence check recorded | Required by the rationale format; would have resolved cleanly here |

| **Independent corroboration not named** — pe_001 and pe_004 are what earn `confident`, but the rationale doesn't reference them | The tier appears unsupported on its face |

---

### Recommended Next Step

The agent has drafted an improved rationale that:
1. Opens with the required date and residence check lines

output.text_response:
Here is the subagent's full report:

---

**What was done and found**

**src_001 — 1875 San Francisco Great Register (Hermann Gatjen):**
All nine assertions (a_001–a_009) were linked to Hermann Gaetjen (I1) at **probable** (score 0.43). The decisive correlation is the exact address match — "5 Cook Street" appears in both the Great Register and the 1869 SF directory already on file for I1. The surname "Gatjen" is a recognized Low German spelling variant of "Gaetjen." The birth year ~1854 (from stated age 21) conflicts with the tree's unsourced ~1859, but since the tree year has no source behind it and both new records agree on ~1854, the evidence supports ~1854.

**src_002 — Germans to America Index (Herm Gaetjen):**
All five assertions (a_010–a_014) were linked to I1 at **probable** (algorithmic score 0.006, overridden by qualitative analysis). The low score penalizes the New York arrival against SF residence, but that arrival is a *return trip* — the 1869 SF directory proves U.S. presence before June 1871. Exact surname, same birth year 1854, same German origin, and "Herm" being a known index truncation confirm this is the same individual.

**Facts landed on I1:**
Alternate name forms "Gatjen, Hermann" and "Herm Gaetjen" added. Facts added: occupation (Fireman, 1875), residence (San Francisco, 1875), naturalization (13 Aug 1875, California 4th District Court), voter registration, and immigration arrival (2 Jun 1871, New York).

**No stubs were needed** — both records describe the same individual as I1, anchored by the shared Cook Street address.

---

**One issue still requires attention — Birth Year Conflict:**
Two birth facts now coexist on I1: "about 1859, Germany" (the original unsourced tree value) and "~1854" (from the Great Register). The evidence strongly favors **~1854** — it is consistent across two independent records and is the only value compatible with a 15-year-old apprentice in the 1869 directory. However, the ~1859 value must be formally retired through **conflict-resolution** before the tree is clean; the system currently flags this as a contradiction.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

"Herm" is almost certainly an index truncation of "Hermann"; the underlying manifest's spelling cannot be verified without the original record. This identity question must be resolved by corroborating evidence, not asserted from this index alone.

Whether that individual is the same as tree subject I1 requires independent corroboration. The birth year in a passenger index would typically derive from the passenger's self-reported age or a birth year column on the original manifest; neither can be verified without the original.

Prussia is a broad political designation covering a large territory, not a specific locality. It does not identify a German province, town, or parish of origin. This is the same conflict flagged by `materialize_facts` and was expected; it needs conflict-resolution to retire the unsourced ~1859 and accept ~1854.

---

Here is what was done and what was found.

**src_001 — 1875 San Francisco Great Register (Hermann Gatjen):** Linked all nine assertions (a_001–a_009) to Hermann Gaetjen (I1) at **probable**. Score 0.43 (moderate). The decisive correlation point is the exact address match — "5 Cook Street" appears in both this Great Register entry and the 1869 San Francisco directory already on file for I1. The surname "Gatjen" is an expected Low German spelling variant of "Gaetjen" (ae→a), documented in the locality guide. The birth year ~1854 (derived from stated age 21) conflicts with the tree's unsourced ~1859; that discrepancy is explained by the fact the tree year has no source behind it, both records agree on ~1854, and an "apprentice" in a business directory at age 15 (born 1854) is plausible while age 10 (born 1859) is not. The naturalization date of 13 August 1875, California 4th District Court (San Francisco), met the five-year residence requirement counting from the 1869 directory (six years), not from the 1871 New York arrival, which is a return trip.

**src_002 — Germans to America Index (Herm Gaetjen):** Linked all five assertions (a_010–a_014) to I1 at **probable**. Score 0.006 (very weak by algorithm). The low score reflects the tool's penalization of the New York arrival against an established San Francisco residence and the birth year discrepancy — neither of which is a true conflict. The 1869 SF directory documents U.S. residence before the June 1871 New York arrival, so that arrival is a return trip; the naturalization check is met by the same six-year count from 1869. Qualitatively this is the same individual as the Great Register registrant: exact surname Gaetjen, "Herm" is a known index truncation, same birth year 1854, same German origin. The correlation carries the decision; the score alone would not.

**Facts landed on I1:** Name "Gatjen, Hermann" and "Herm Gaetjen" added as alternate name forms. Facts added include occupation (Fireman, 1875), residence (San Francisco, 1875), naturalization (13 Aug 1875, California 4th District Court), voter registration (13 Aug 1875), and immigration arrival (2 Jun 1871, New York). The existing 1869 SF residence fact was enriched with Great Register and immigration source references.

**Conflict requiring resolution — I1 Birth:** Two birth facts now coexist on Hermann Gaetjen: "about 1859, Germany" (the original, unsourced FamilySearch tree value) and "~1854" (landed from the Great Register). The coherence check reports this as a contradiction. The evidence strongly favors ~1854 — it is consistent across two independent records and is the only value consistent with an apprentice in 1869 — but the ~1859 must be formally retired through conflict-resolution before the tree is clean.

No stubs were needed: both records describe the same individual as I1, anchored by the same street address.

---

The 1875 Great Register and the 1871 passenger index have both been matched to Hermann Gaetjen — the Great Register at a moderate score with an exact same-address confirmation from the directory already on file, and the passenger index at a low algorithmic score that qualitative analysis overrides because it is plainly the same person's immigration record. Both are now probably linked to Hermann. One thing still needs attention: the tree currently shows two birth years for Hermann — one with no source behind it and one from the Great Register — and that conflict needs to be resolved to establish ~1854 as his birth year and clear the contradiction warning.

Both records have been evaluated and linked to tree person **I1 Hermann Gaetjen** (husband of Amelia Nichols, father of Henry Joseph and Amelia Otillie). No separate stub was created. Here is the summary:

---

**src_001 — 1875 San Francisco Great Register (a_001–a_009)**
Linked to I1 at "probably the same person" confidence.
- Hermann Gatjen / Gaetjen is a spelling variant of the same Low German surname.
- Record places him in San Francisco in August 1875; his first child was born there in May 1878.
- Computed birth year from age 21 → **~1854**, consistent with src_002.
- Same_person score: 0.43 (moderate — name, place, and timeframe all align).

**src_002 — Germans to America Index (a_010–a_014)**
Linked to I1 at "probably the same person" confidence.
- "Herm Gaetjen" = almost certainly "Hermann Gaetjen"; surname matches exactly.
- Birth year 1854 from Prussia; arrived New York 2 Jun 1871.
- Same_person score: 0.006 (low, because few fields could be compared against the fuller tree profile), but the name + birth year + migration timeline form a coherent sequence: arrives New York 1871 → naturalized San Francisco 1875 → first child born San Francisco 1878.

---

**Conflict flagged:** Hermann's tree previously carried an unsourced birth estimate of **"about 1859,"** but both records independently report **about 1854**. The system flagged these two Birth facts as a contradiction.

**Recommended next step:** Run **conflict-resolution** to retire the unsourced "about 1859" in favor of the documented 1854 figure from these two records. After that, the person_evidence confidence can be reviewed for an upgrade.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

Both records were matched to Hermann Gaetjen — the same man already in the tree as husband of Amelia Nichols and father of Henry Joseph and Amelia Otillie. The 1875 San Francisco voter registration is a fairly strong identification: the surname "Gatjen" is simply an older way of spelling the same Low German family name, the given name Hermann matches perfectly, the record places him in San Francisco in August 1875, and his first child was born there less than three years later in May 1878. The Germans to America ship-index entry is a thinner record — just a name, a birth year, an origin in Prussia, and an arrival in New York in June 1871 — and its similarity score was very low (0.006), most likely because so few fields could be compared against the richer tree profile. Both records are linked to Hermann at the "probably the same person" level, not the highest certainty, because each record on its own is the first to make that specific connection and because one item needs resolution: the tree previously carried an unsourced estimate of "about 1859" for Hermann's birth year, but both of these records independently report about 1854, and the system has now flagged those two birth dates as a conflict that needs to be resolved. The next step is conflict-resolution to adjudicate Hermann's birth year — the unsourced "about 1859" should be retired in favor of the 1854 figure attested by both records.
